raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by myocardial deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils, most commonly immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloid and transthyretin amyloid (ATTR) [1]. AL-CA is a hematologic emergency because circulating monoclonal light chains are directly cardiotoxic and survival may be measured in months when advanced heart failure is present [1]. ATTR-CA results either from age-related wild-type transthyretin deposition (ATTRwt) or pathogenic TTR variants (ATTRv), with phenotypes spanning restrictive cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, autonomic dysfunction, and conduction disease [2]. Contemporary reviews emphasize that CA is no longer rare in specialist practice, largely because noninvasive imaging has improved recognition [3]. Natural-history cohorts show that AL, ATTRv, and ATTRwt have distinct trajectories and therapeutic implications, making accurate typing essential [4].

Epidemiologically, ATTRwt predominantly affects older men and often presents as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial arrhythmias, low-flow aortic stenosis, or unexplained increased ventricular wall thickness [5]. Screening studies have identified ATTRwt among patients labelled as having HFpEF [6] and among elderly patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis [7]. Autopsy data suggest that transthyretin cardiac deposition is frequent in the very old, although not always clinically apparent [8]. ATTRv prevalence varies markedly by ancestry and geography; targeted evaluation of patients with unexplained hypertrophy can reveal hereditary disease, with implications for cascade testing [9].

Diagnosis begins with clinical suspicion. Red flags include discordance between increased wall thickness and low QRS voltage, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, biceps tendon rupture, spinal stenosis, nephrotic-range proteinuria, macroglossia, periorbital purpura, autonomic symptoms, and intolerance of standard heart-failure drugs. The central diagnostic step is to exclude AL amyloidosis using serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation; if any monoclonal abnormality is present, tissue confirmation and amyloid typing are usually required. In patients without monoclonal protein, grade 2–3 cardiac uptake on bone-avid scintigraphy permits a nonbiopsy diagnosis of ATTR-CA [10]. Technetium-99m pyrophosphate imaging differentiates ATTR from AL with high accuracy when interpreted with monoclonal testing [11], building on earlier work with technetium-DPD scintigraphy [12]. Expert consensus recommends standardized acquisition, visual grading, semiquantitative heart-to-contralateral ratios, and avoidance of false positives from blood pool activity or myocardial infarction [13].

Echocardiography remains a first-line test, typically showing concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, valve thickening, restrictive filling, and pericardial effusion. Strain imaging may show “relative apical sparing,” a useful clue but not a stand-alone diagnostic criterion [17]. Cardiac magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, increased native T1, and expanded extracellular volume support the diagnosis and quantify burden [14-16]. Endomyocardial biopsy remains the gold standard when noninvasive findings are discordant, AL is possible, or rare amyloid types are suspected.

Risk stratification is biomarker-driven. In AL amyloidosis, troponin and natriuretic peptides reflect cardiac injury and wall stress and form the basis of staging systems [20,21]. Hematologic response, particularly reduction in involved free light chains, translates into improved organ outcomes and survival [19]. CMR T1 mapping also has prognostic value in systemic AL amyloidosis [18]. In ATTRwt, staging systems using natriuretic peptides, troponin, and renal function help estimate prognosis [22,23], but frailty, conduction disease, atrial fibrillation, and extracardiac involvement should also inform decisions.

Management has two parallel aims: supportive cardiovascular care and amyloid-directed therapy. Diuretics are the cornerstone for congestion, often requiring careful titration because stroke volume is fixed and renal function is vulnerable. Beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are frequently poorly tolerated; anticoagulation is generally favored for atrial fibrillation and may be considered at low thresholds because atrial mechanical dysfunction is common. Pacemakers treat bradyarrhythmias, while defibrillator benefit is uncertain in advanced restrictive disease.

Disease-modifying treatment depends on amyloid type. Tafamidis stabilizes transthyretin and reduces mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization in ATTR cardiomyopathy [24]. Diflunisal also stabilizes TTR but is limited by renal, gastrointestinal, and fluid-retention toxicity [25]. Gene-silencing therapies, including patisiran and inotersen, reduce hepatic transthyretin production and improve neuropathy; cardiac endpoints and cardiomyopathy-specific trials have expanded their relevance [26,27]. In vivo TTR gene editing is an emerging strategy with early evidence of profound transthyretin reduction [28]. For AL amyloidosis, prompt plasma-cell therapy is essential. Bortezomib-based regimens rapidly suppress light-chain production [29], and daratumumab added to cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone improves hematologic and organ responses [30]. Overall, CA has shifted from a late, biopsy-dependent diagnosis to a treatable cardiomyopathy in which early recognition, precise typing, and timely therapy determine outcome.
